title: From one curve to the ingredients: why restricted Hartree-Fock fails at dissociation, what an orbital looks like, and what J and K are
summary: Three course figures cover the basic vocabulary of electronic structure. The H2 energy curve compares methods against the exact (full CI) answer in a minimal setting; polar plots show the angular shape of s and p orbitals; two small matrices list the Coulomb and exchange integrals that enter every Hartree-Fock energy.

media.alt: Two panels. Left, panel a titled whole curve: energy relative to two hydrogen atoms in kcal per mole against H-H distance from 0.5 to 3.7 angstrom, with five curves: full CI as black dots, RHF in red rising steeply, UHF dashed yellow levelling to zero, a blue harmonic spring that rises very steeply, a green dotted Morse curve close to full CI. Right, panel b zooms on the minimum between 0.55 and 1.15 angstrom.

read_the_figure.question: Which method reproduces the true curve near the minimum and at long distance, and what do the failures tell us about the method?
read_the_figure.axes: H2 curve: horizontal, H-H distance in angstrom; vertical, energy relative to two separated H atoms in kcal/mol (negative is bound). Polar plots: angle around the circle, radius equal to the size of the angular function. Matrices: row and column are the two spatial orbitals g and u; colour and number give the integral in hartree.
look_at: Panel a: the black full CI curve is the reference. It dips to about -104 kcal/mol near 0.75 angstrom and returns to zero at long distance.

RHF (solid red) is far too high at stretched geometries and crosses zero near 1.5 angstrom, rising to +60 and beyond: it forces both electrons into the same spatial orbital, which at long distance contains a large ionic component.

UHF (dashed yellow) goes to zero at long distance, because breaking the spin symmetry lets the electrons separate; it is also shallow at the minimum (about -82 kcal/mol in panel b), the same as RHF there.

The blue harmonic spring (a force field) is accurate only in a narrow window at the bottom and climbs far too steeply; the green Morse curve with the same stiffness and depth follows full CI to within a few kcal/mol over the whole range.

Orbital shapes: s has no angular dependence (a circle); p_z has two lobes of opposite sign along z; p_x has two lobes along x. Panels 1 and 2 plot the angle theta, panel 3 plots phi, so their orientations are not comparable.
J and K matrices: the diagonal entries are identical in the two matrices (0.6746 and 0.6975); off-diagonals differ, J_gu = 0.6636 against K_gu = 0.1813.
read_the_figure.proves: The curve shows that a method can be right at one geometry and wrong at another, so a single energy at the minimum cannot validate it. The J and K matrices show a general identity (J_pp = K_pp) and the strong reduction of exchange for orbitals of different symmetry.
if_wrong: A curve that goes up at long distance instead of to zero: single-determinant restricted treatment of bond breaking.
A method that agrees at the minimum and disagrees at 2 angstrom: the shape of the potential, not only the depth, must be checked.
Orbital lobes drawn without sign: the sign (phase) is what decides bonding or antibonding combinations.
Off-diagonal K larger than J: not possible; check the integral definitions.
must_check: That the reference (full CI) is drawn with the same basis as the approximate methods.
That energy is relative to the separated atoms, so all curves share a zero.
That angular plots say which angle is plotted and which plane is cut.
That integrals are labelled J or K and the units (hartree) given.

terms.meaning: The exact solution within the chosen basis: all electron configurations are included.
Hartree-Fock with each spatial orbital doubly occupied (restricted) or with different orbitals for the two spins (unrestricted).
A three-parameter bond model with the correct dissociation limit.
The part of an orbital that depends on direction; for s it is constant, for p proportional to cos theta.
J is the repulsion between two charge clouds; K is the same with the electrons swapped between orbitals.

remember: Hartree-Fock energy is a sum of one-electron terms and J minus K terms.
Full CI within a basis is exact for that basis; method errors are measured against it.
A harmonic spring has no dissociation limit; a Morse curve does.
p orbitals have a node: a plane where the wave function is zero and changes sign.
Always J_pp = K_pp, and K_pq <= sqrt(J_pp J_qq).

steps.title: A Morse curve in kcal per mole
steps.note: With the same force constant k at the minimum and the same depth D as the exact curve, the Morse curve has the right curvature and the right limit. Expand near r_e to recover the harmonic spring V = k (r - r_e)^2 / 2 - D.

steps.title: Why the restricted wave function dissociates wrongly
steps.note: The product of the same bonding orbital for both electrons contains covalent and ionic terms with equal weight. At long distance the ionic part is too high in energy, so the curve rises above the two-atom limit.

steps.title: The angular shapes
steps.note: A polar plot of |cos theta| is two circles tangent at the origin: the two lobes of the middle panel. The sign change at the origin is the nodal plane; the colour change from red to yellow in the figure marks it.

steps.title: Coulomb and exchange for two orbitals
steps.note: For p = q the two integrals coincide, which is why the diagonals of the two matrices match. For p different from q, K is smaller because the overlap density phi_p phi_q has positive and negative parts that largely cancel.

worked.title: Check the bounds on the J and K entries
worked.problem: From the matrices: J_gg = 0.674594, J_uu = 0.697495, K_gu = 0.181258, J_gu = 0.663564. Check K_gu <= sqrt(J_gg J_uu) and J_gu <= the same bound.
worked.answer: Both entries satisfy the bound; J_gu is close to it, K_gu is far below it.

analyze.q: Why does UHF reach zero energy at long distance but give the same minimum depth as RHF in panel b?
analyze.hint: At the minimum the unrestricted solution is the restricted one.

evaluate.q: A new method matches full CI to 1 kcal/mol at 0.75 angstrom. Is that enough to adopt it? What else would you ask for?
The orbital figure plots two different angles. Why is that a caution about comparing panels?

checks.q: What is the dashed line at zero in panel a?
checks.answer: The energy of two separated hydrogen atoms; every curve is measured from it.

checks.q: Morse depth 104 kcal/mol, force constant k: how does a depend on k?
checks.answer: a grows as the square root of k: a stiffer bond gives a narrower well.

checks.q: Why is RHF too high at 2 angstrom?
checks.answer: Its wave function is half ionic (H+ H-) at any distance, which is high in energy when the atoms are far apart.

checks.q: Is it fair to compare a force-field curve with quantum methods at all geometries?
checks.answer: Only near the minimum: a harmonic force field is built for small displacements and has no dissociation limit.

checks.q: Design a figure that would reveal symmetry breaking in UHF at a glance.
checks.answer: Add a lower panel of the spin-squared expectation value against distance; it departs from zero where the symmetry breaks.
